analysis.one_liner: Caps what drug makers can charge for medications at the lowest price other developed countries pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2023 with no cosponsors, sent to six House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Department to set a maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the lowest price the drug sells for in eleven developed countries including Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and Canada. That ceiling would apply to Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, TRICARE, the VA, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, and Indian Health Service care. Drug makers would also have to offer the same capped price to uninsured people and to people with private insurance, and face a civil penalty of five times the overcharge if they didn't comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, military families, veterans, federal employees, tribal health patients, uninsured people, and privately insured people all pay less for prescription drugs. Penalty money collected from manufacturers that charge too much would go to the National Institutes of Health for drug research.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the retail list price of every prescription drug under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, and Indian Health Service programs at a government-set reference price.

Sets the reference price at the lowest price the drug sells for among eleven reference countries (Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden) when pricing data is available for at least three of them.

Requires manufacturers to offer drugs at the reference price to everyone, including uninsured individuals and people with employer or private insurance, so the price cap reaches beyond federal programs.
Imposes a civil penalty of five times the amount a manufacturer overcharged under federal health programs, and directs the money to NIH for drug research and development.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers would see their US prices pulled down toward international levels, reducing revenue that funds their research and development budgets. To the extent lower drug prices flow through, insurers and employers would also pay less in claims costs.

drawbacks.text: Tying US prices to the lowest price in eleven countries would cut manufacturer revenue, and the pharmaceutical industry argues that reduced revenue means less investment in researching new drugs, though how large that effect would be is disputed.

The civil penalty only counts overcharges on federal-program sales, so a manufacturer charging uninsured or privately insured patients above the reference price faces no direct penalty under the enforcement formula.

For drugs where pricing data is unavailable in at least three reference countries, the price would be set by a subjective HHS judgment of the drug's value and development costs, which creates uncertainty about how the cap would actually be calculated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is direct and large: every prescription drug would be priced at no more than what eleven peer countries pay, and the cap reaches people outside federal programs. The cost falls on drug makers' revenue, and the strongest honest objection is that lower revenue could slow the development of future medicines. That tradeoff is real but heavily weighted toward patients, since existing prices in the US are consistently far above the reference countries' prices. The enforcement gap for non-federal sales is a design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six committees and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee three separate times, but no committee ever held a markup or a vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced the bill in the House on June 20, 2023.
The bill was referred to six House committees at once: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Accountability, and Natural Resources.
No cosponsors ever signed on, so the bill entered committee with a single sponsor.
The bill was referred to the Health Subcommittee in June 2023, July 2023, and December 2024, but no full committee or subcommittee action followed, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill never advanced: they keep charging US prices well above what the same drugs sell for in peer countries, and Medicare, Medicaid, veterans, and privately insured patients keep paying them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, who keep US prices

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap prescription drug prices at reference-country levels and pursued it through the committee process; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and referred it to its Health Subcommittee, but never scheduled a markup or a vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight, and Natural Resources Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for portions within their jurisdiction and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so there is no roll-call record, but the bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors in a House controlled by Republicans, and international reference pricing is a position that divides the parties.

industries.note: The bill caps what they can charge for every drug at the lowest price paid in eleven peer countries, and requires them to offer that price to privately insured and uninsured patients too. US prices for the same drugs are typically far higher, so this would directly cut revenue that American patients currently pay.

The reference price applies to generic and biosimilar drugs as well, but generics generally already sell at lower prices, so the cap would have little effect on them while lower prices overall could expand access.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers who fund coverage
industries.note: With the price cap reaching group and individual insurance plans, insurers and employers would pay less in drug claims, reducing premiums and coverage costs for workers.
